R-117: a Point's WIDTH was gated by CL-BUG-095 (commit ea79620a); its two COORDINATES were never gated to be field elements. decomposePoint / cDecomposePoint BIN2NUM each half of the blob as an unsigned integer, so any width-fitting value is accepted -- x + p included, whenever x + p < 2^(8w). Field arithmetic downstream reduces mod p, so (x+p)||y behaves ARITHMETICALLY as the point (x, y), but affineAdd's two case selectors are bare OP_NUMEQUAL on the RAW decomposed values and do not reduce:  cond = (px == qx) AND (py == qy), notinf = NOT(px == qx AND NOT cond). For P and its alias both read 0, so the chord path runs on two equal points with den_chord = qx - px = 0 (mod p) and a Fermat inverse where inv(0) = 0.

REPRODUCED BY EXECUTION on @bsv/sdk's Spend with real secp256k1, before the fix, using the smallest-x secp256k1 point P = (1, 4218f20a...7e76a7ee) and P' = (1 + p, same y):

    ecAdd(P, P')  -> fffffffe...81895441    x = p-2, i.e. -2x, and OFF CURVE
A script that SUCCEEDED and returned a blob that is not a point, for an input that denotes P + P. Both the R-052 doubling fix and the R-053 P + (-P) fix are driven by these same two selectors, so both are defeated by the same trick. The same reproduction runs on P-256 (x = 5) and P-384 (x = 2), where x + p likewise fits in the coordinate width.

----- SECTION (2026-09-15, R-156 ecMakePoint field-element gate) -----

R-156: `ecMakePoint(x, y)` was NOT INJECTIVE. Per coordinate it emitted `push 33, OP_NUM2BIN, push 32, OP_SPLIT, OP_DROP`. NUM2BIN(33) writes a 33-byte little-endian SIGN-MAGNITUDE script number, so byte 32 is exactly where the sign bit lives AND where any bits >= 2^256 land -- and the split drops precisely that byte.

REPRODUCED BY EXECUTION on @bsv/sdk's Spend, before the fix, with the secp256k1 point (1, 4218f20a...7e76a7ee):
    ecMakePoint( 1n, y)          -> 0000...0001 || 4218f20a...
    ecMakePoint(-1n, y)          -> the SAME bytes      (sign discarded)
    ecMakePoint(1n + 2^256, y)   -> the SAME bytes      (magnitude truncated)
    ecMakePoint( 1n, -y)         -> the SAME bytes      (and on the y half)
The y-half collision is the sharpest of the three: `ecMakePoint(x, 0n - y)` is how a contract author spells point negation by hand, and it silently produced (x, +y) -- the point being negated -- rather than (x, p-y) or an error.

THIS IS NOT COVERED BY R-117 and cannot be. The bytes ecMakePoint emits for -1n are the perfectly canonical encoding of 1, so the coordinate-canonicity gate on ecAdd / ecMul / ecNegate sees a well-formed Point and has nothing to reject. The aliasing happens before any Point exists. The two findings are independent, which is why they are separate commits.

THE FIX REJECTS: each coordinate must satisfy 0 <= v < p, checked with OP_WITHIN and OP_VERIFY -- the same half-open bound the `within` builtin exposes to authors, in one opcode. Reducing mod p was considered and rejected for the reason R-117 gives: ecOnCurve answers "no" to a coordinate outside [0, p), so reducing here would leave the constructor and the predicate disagreeing about what a point is. Rejecting also restores INJECTIVITY, which is the property the defect broke.

----- SECTION (2026-09-15, R-157 ecMul on-curve-or-infinity gate) -----

R-157: the ladder's correctness argument holds only for points ON the curve, every tier wrote that down, and nothing enforced it.

`ecMul(P, k)` does not compute k*P. It computes ((k mod n) + 3n)*P: the MSB-first ladder adds 3n so that a fixed high bit is always set, and +3n is a NO-OP ONLY WHEN ord(P) DIVIDES n. Cofactor 1 gives ord(P) = n for every point on the curve, so the trick is sound there and nowhere else. A point off the curve lies on some other curve y^2 = x^3 + b' whose order is unrelated to n, and the whole computation silently answers a different question.

REPRODUCED BY EXECUTION on @bsv/sdk's Spend, before the fix, with the off-curve point P = (5, 7), which lies on y^2 = x^3 - 76:
    ecMul(P, 1n)  ->  c8b039d1...9438f2ff   which is NOT P
    ecMul(P, 2n)  ->  e673c72b...c8dde4c8   which is NOT 2P
Both match ((k mod n) + 3n)*P computed off-chain on that other curve EXACTLY, which is how the mechanism was identified rather than guessed. `ecMul(P, 1n) != P` is the whole finding: the primitive violated its own contract for every off-curve input, not merely a contrived one.

The degenerate sub-case is worse. For a 2-torsion point of the other curve -- any (x, 0) -- every multiple collapses to the all-zero blob, measured for k = 1, 2, 3, 5, because the ladder's unguarded mixed-add hits H = R = 0 mid-ladder, sets Z3 = 0, and a Jacobian accumulator at infinity can never leave it. Combined with R-053 -- which correctly taught ecAdd that the all-zero blob is the identity -- that turns a Schnorr-shaped s*G == R + e*P verifier into a free pass: choose an off-curve P of order 2, e*P is O, R + O is R, and any s with R = s*G verifies with no knowledge of any discrete log. R-053 is right and is not being undone; this is the other half of the same seam.

WHY THE GATE BELONGS IN ecMul AND NOT IN THE CALLER. The +3n offset is INTERNAL to ecMul: a caller cannot see it, cannot know the obligation exists without reading the codegen, and gains nothing by checking what ecMul can check more cheaply (ecOnCurve is 816 bytes against ecMul's 428,754 -- 0.19%). The obligation WAS written down, in all seven tiers, in buildJacobianAddOrDoubleInline's own docstring: "callers who accept untrusted points must gate them on ecOnCurve first". Nothing enforced it, and the repository's own schnorr-zkp fixture takes its pubKey from a DEPLOYER-supplied constructor slot, where that idiom is not even reachable.

WHY NOT ecAdd, which is the other half of the boundary: affineAdd implements the group law with no n-dependent trick, so on an off-curve operand it returns the CORRECT sum on that operand's own curve -- it does not lie. And O, which is deliberately not on the curve, must keep flowing through ecAdd for R-053 to hold. Gating the adder would break a working primitive to fix a different one.

O IS EXEMPTED and the exemption is load-bearing: ecMul(P, 0n) returns the all-zero blob, ecAdd(P, -P) returns it, and the EC optimizer folds to it, so O is a reachable runtime operand -- while ecOnCurve(O) is false by construction (0^2 != 0^3 + b). A bare on-curve gate would reject the identity this codegen manufactures itself. The gate is therefore `onCurve(P) OR P == O`.

  (1) packages/runar-testing/src/__tests__/r157-ecmul-curve-gate.test.ts executes every claim on @bsv/sdk's Spend across all three curves -- 28 assertions, 7 RED before the fix and GREEN after. Controls with teeth, all of which must stay green and would redden on an over-strict gate: mul(G, k) still works and lands on the curve; mul(G, 1) is G; mulGen(k) agrees with mul(G, k); mul(O, k) is still O for every k WHILE ecOnCurve(O) is false, which is exactly why a bare on-curve gate would not do; mul(P, 0n) still produces O; and ecAdd(G, O) = G, the deliberately-ungated half of the boundary.
  (2) Every tier was falsified individually: neutering the gate in one tier and rebuilding that tier's binary makes it, and only it, the lone outlier against the other six on ec-unit. Seven for seven.
  (3) All seven independently written compilers produce these exact bytes. Before regeneration the conformance run reported 0 IR/script mismatches BETWEEN compilers and 49 golden mismatches = 7 fixtures x 7 tiers, unanimous.
  (4) An exhaustive sweep of all 78 fixtures -- compiled, not grepped -- shows exactly 7 move and 71 byte-unchanged. p256-wallet, p384-wallet and r1-k1-wallet are again byte-unchanged, which is the measured confirmation that the gate is on the PUBLIC pNNNMul builtins and not inside the ladder shared with verifyECDSA -- where decompressPubKey and the signature range gate have already decided that attacker-chosen bytes must yield `false` from a total boolean builtin rather than abort. expected-ir.json does not move.
  (5) conformance/witnesses/real-crypto-execution.test.ts re-executes the moved fixtures' spends through a second engine and is green.

COST: +12558 bytes total, +0.14% to +0.20% per fixture, 805 bytes per secp256k1 ecMul call site.

WHY NOT ecAdd, which is the other half of the boundary: affineAdd implements the group law with no n-dependent trick, so on an off-curve operand it returns the CORRECT sum on that operand's own curve -- it does not lie. The obligation WAS written down, in all seven tiers, in buildJacobianAddOrDoubleInline's own docstring: "callers who accept untrusted points must gate them on ecOnCurve first". Nothing enforced it, and the repository's own schnorr-zkp fixture takes its pubKey from a DEPLOYER-supplied constructor slot, where that idiom is not even reachable.

WHY NOT ecAdd, which is the other half of the boundary: affineAdd implements the group law with no n-dependent trick, so on an off-curve operand it returns the CORRECT sum on that operand's own curve -- it does not lie. And O, which is deliberately not on the curve, must keep flowing through ecAdd for R-053 to hold. Gating the adder would break a working primitive to fix a different one.

O IS EXEMPTED and the exemption is load-bearing: ecMul(P, 0n) returns the all-zero blob, ecAdd(P, -P) returns it, and the EC optimizer folds to it, so O is a reachable runtime operand -- while ecOnCurve(O) is false by construction (0^2 != 0^3 + b). A bare on-curve gate would reject the identity this codegen manufactures itself. The gate is therefore `onCurve(P) OR P == O`.

  (1) packages/runar-testing/src/__tests__/r157-ecmul-curve-gate.test.ts executes every claim on @bsv/sdk's Spend across all three curves -- 28 assertions, 7 RED before the fix and GREEN after. Controls with teeth, all of which must stay green and would redden on an over-strict gate: mul(G, k) still works and lands on the curve; mul(G, 1) is G; mulGen(k) agrees with mul(G, k); mul(O, k) is still O for every k WHILE ecOnCurve(O) is false, which is exactly why a bare on-curve gate would not do; mul(P, 0n) still produces O; and ecAdd(G, O) = G, the deliberately-ungated half of the boundary.
  (2) Every tier was falsified individually: neutering the gate in one tier and rebuilding that tier's binary makes it, and only it, the lone outlier against the other six on ec-unit. Seven for seven.
  (3) All seven independently written compilers produce these exact bytes. Before regeneration the conformance run reported 0 IR/script mismatches BETWEEN compilers and 49 golden mismatches = 7 fixtures x 7 tiers, unanimous.
  (4) An exhaustive sweep of all 78 fixtures -- compiled, not grepped -- shows exactly 7 move and 71 byte-unchanged. p256-wallet, p384-wallet and r1-k1-wallet are again byte-unchanged, which is the measured confirmation that the gate is on the PUBLIC pNNNMul builtins and not inside the ladder shared with verifyECDSA -- where decompressPubKey and the signature range gate have already decided that attacker-chosen bytes must yield `false` from a total boolean builtin rather than abort. expected-ir.json does not move.

WHY THE NEW SIZE IS CORRECT. R-169 as filed covered pow AND sqrt; commit a3c4c0af fixed sqrt and changed zero lines mentioning pow. lowerPow unrolled exactly 32 conditional multiplies with NO guard on the exponent, so it computed base^min(exp, 32) and returned that CLAMPED value with no error for any larger exponent -- measured on @bsv/sdk Spend: pow(2,33) = 4294967296, pow(2,40) = 4294967296, pow(3,50) = 1853020188851841 (= 3^32), pow(2,-1) = 1. Every tier clamped identically, so cross-tier hex parity was green on the wrong answer. The constant folder computed the TRUE power for 0 <= exp <= 256 and the reference interpreter is exact for every exp >= 0, so inside the window 33 <= exp <= 256 the same source compiled fold-ON and fold-OFF produced scripts accepting MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE inputs.

The fix mirrors what sqrt got twenty lines away in the same files: the domain is ENFORCED rather than documented. lowerPow now emits, once per callsite, on the exponent:

    OP_DUP <0> <33> OP_WITHIN OP_VERIFY

= OP_DUP(1) + OP_0(1) + push 33 as 0x01 0x21(2) + OP_WITHIN(1) + OP_VERIFY(1) = 6 bytes. The constant folder's bound goes 256 -> 32 and the reference interpreter throws above 32, so all three implementations now refuse on exactly the same boundary.

The bound stays 32 rather than rising to the folder's old 256. That is a measured decision, not an omission: each extra unrolled round costs 8-9 script bytes AT EVERY CALLSITE (~2 KB to reach 256), and a raised bound would STILL need a guard at the new limit -- it moves the cliff rather than removing it.

  (2) The same file pins fold agreement in BOTH modes via runFoldEquivalence, including every exponent in the old 33..256 bug window, where each case previously reported two divergences with the two modes accepting different values.

----- SECTION (2026-09-15, R-157 ecMul on-curve-or-infinity gate) -----

R-157: the ladder's correctness argument holds only for points ON the curve, every tier wrote that down, and nothing enforced it.

`ecMul(P, k)` does not compute k*P. It computes ((k mod n) + 3n)*P: the MSB-first ladder adds 3n so that a fixed high bit is always set, and +3n is a NO-OP ONLY WHEN ord(P) DIVIDES n. Cofactor 1 gives ord(P) = n for every point on the curve, so the trick is sound there and nowhere else. A point off the curve lies on some other curve y^2 = x^3 + b' whose order is unrelated to n, and the whole computation silently answers a different question.

REPRODUCED BY EXECUTION on @bsv/sdk's Spend, before the fix, with the off-curve point P = (5, 7), which lies on y^2 = x^3 - 76:
    ecMul(P, 1n)  ->  c8b039d1...9438f2ff   which is NOT P
    ecMul(P, 2n)  ->  e673c72b...c8dde4c8   which is NOT 2P
Both match ((k mod n) + 3n)*P computed off-chain on that other curve EXACTLY, which is how the mechanism was identified rather than guessed. `ecMul(P, 1n) != P` is the whole finding: the primitive violated its own contract for every off-curve input, not merely a contrived one.

The degenerate sub-case is worse. For a 2-torsion point of the other curve -- any (x, 0) -- every multiple collapses to the all-zero blob, measured for k = 1, 2, 3, 5, because the ladder's unguarded mixed-add hits H = R = 0 mid-ladder, sets Z3 = 0, and a Jacobian accumulator at infinity can never leave it. Combined with R-053 -- which correctly taught ecAdd that the all-zero blob is the identity -- that turns a Schnorr-shaped s*G == R + e*P verifier into a free pass: choose an off-curve P of order 2, e*P is O, R + O is R, and any s with R = s*G verifies with no knowledge of any discrete log. R-053 is right and is not being undone; this is the other half of the same seam.

WHY THE GATE BELONGS IN ecMul AND NOT IN THE CALLER. The +3n offset is INTERNAL to ecMul: a caller cannot see it, cannot know the obligation exists without reading the codegen, and gains nothing by checking what ecMul can check more cheaply (ecOnCurve is 816 bytes against ecMul's 428,754 -- 0.19%). The obligation WAS written down, in all seven tiers, in buildJacobianAddOrDoubleInline's own docstring: "callers who accept untrusted points must gate them on ecOnCurve first". Nothing enforced it, and the repository's own schnorr-zkp fixture takes its pubKey from a DEPLOYER-supplied constructor slot, where that idiom is not even reachable.

WHY NOT ecAdd, which is the other half of the boundary: affineAdd implements the group law with no n-dependent trick, so on an off-curve operand it returns the CORRECT sum on that operand's own curve -- it does not lie. And O, which is deliberately not on the curve, must keep flowing through ecAdd for R-053 to hold. Gating the adder would break a working primitive to fix a different one.

O IS EXEMPTED and the exemption is load-bearing: ecMul(P, 0n) returns the all-zero blob, ecAdd(P, -P) returns it, and the EC optimizer folds to it, so O is a reachable runtime operand -- while ecOnCurve(O) is false by construction (0^2 != 0^3 + b). A bare on-curve gate would reject the identity this codegen manufactures itself. The gate is therefore `onCurve(P) OR P == O`.

Controls with teeth, all of which must stay green and would redden on an over-strict gate: mul(G, k) still works and lands on the curve; mul(G, 1) is G; mulGen(k) agrees with mul(G, k); mul(O, k) is still O for every k WHILE ecOnCurve(O) is false, which is exactly why a bare on-curve gate would not do; mul(P, 0n) still produces O; and ecAdd(G, O) = G, the deliberately-ungated half of the boundary.
  (2) Every tier was falsified individually: neutering the gate in one tier and rebuilding that tier's binary makes it, and only it, the lone outlier against the other six on ec-unit. Seven for seven.
  (3) All seven independently written compilers produce these exact bytes. Before regeneration the conformance run reported 0 IR/script mismatches BETWEEN compilers and 49 golden mismatches = 7 fixtures x 7 tiers, unanimous.

----- SECTION (2026-09-15, R-157 ecMul on-curve-or-infinity gate) -----

R-157: the ladder's correctness argument holds only for points ON the curve, every tier wrote that down, and nothing enforced it.

`ecMul(P, k)` does not compute k*P. It computes ((k mod n) + 3n)*P: the MSB-first ladder adds 3n so that a fixed high bit is always set, and +3n is a NO-OP ONLY WHEN ord(P) DIVIDES n. Cofactor 1 gives ord(P) = n for every point on the curve, so the trick is sound there and nowhere else. A point off the curve lies on some other curve y^2 = x^3 + b' whose order is unrelated to n, and the whole computation silently answers a different question.

REPRODUCED BY EXECUTION on @bsv/sdk's Spend, before the fix, with the off-curve point P = (5, 7), which lies on y^2 = x^3 - 76:
    ecMul(P, 1n)  ->  c8b039d1...9438f2ff   which is NOT P
    ecMul(P, 2n)  ->  e673c72b...c8dde4c8   which is NOT 2P
Both match ((k mod n) + 3n)*P computed off-chain on that other curve EXACTLY, which is how the mechanism was identified rather than guessed. `ecMul(P, 1n) != P` is the whole finding: the primitive violated its own contract for every off-curve input, not merely a contrived one.

The degenerate sub-case is worse. For a 2-torsion point of the other curve -- any (x, 0) -- every multiple collapses to the all-zero blob, measured for k = 1, 2, 3, 5, because the ladder's unguarded mixed-add hits H = R = 0 mid-ladder, sets Z3 = 0, and a Jacobian accumulator at infinity can never leave it. Combined with R-053 -- which correctly taught ecAdd that the all-zero blob is the identity -- that turns a Schnorr-shaped s*G == R + e*P verifier into a free pass: choose an off-curve P of order 2, e*P is O, R + O is R, and any s with R = s*G verifies with no knowledge of any discrete log. R-053 is right and is not being undone; this is the other half of the same seam.

WHY THE GATE BELONGS IN ecMul AND NOT IN THE CALLER. The +3n offset is INTERNAL to ecMul: a caller cannot see it, cannot know the obligation exists without reading the codegen, and gains nothing by checking what ecMul can check more cheaply (ecOnCurve is 816 bytes against ecMul's 428,754 -- 0.19%). The obligation WAS written down, in all seven tiers, in buildJacobianAddOrDoubleInline's own docstring: "callers who accept untrusted points must gate them on ecOnCurve first". Nothing enforced it, and the repository's own schnorr-zkp fixture takes its pubKey from a DEPLOYER-supplied constructor slot, where that idiom is not even reachable.

WHY NOT ecAdd, which is the other half of the boundary: affineAdd implements the group law with no n-dependent trick, so on an off-curve operand it returns the CORRECT sum on that operand's own curve -- it does not lie. And O, which is deliberately not on the curve, must keep flowing through ecAdd for R-053 to hold. Gating the adder would break a working primitive to fix a different one.

O IS EXEMPTED and the exemption is load-bearing: ecMul(P, 0n) returns the all-zero blob, ecAdd(P, -P) returns it, and the EC optimizer folds to it, so O is a reachable runtime operand -- while ecOnCurve(O) is false by construction (0^2 != 0^3 + b). A bare on-curve gate would reject the identity this codegen manufactures itself. The gate is therefore `onCurve(P) OR P == O`.

----- SECTION 2 (2026-09-15, R-135 WOTS+ signature-length gate) -----

R-135: verifyWOTS shipped with NO signature-length gate. The emitted verifier consumes the signature 32 bytes at a time with OP_SPLIT, 67 times, then dropped whatever was left over — the TS emitter's own comment said "drop empty sigRest" without ever checking that it was empty. REPRODUCED BY EXECUTION before any byte was touched, not inferred from the opcodes: packages/runar-testing r135-wots-length-gate.test.ts runs the compiled locking script on @bsv/sdk's Spend interpreter, and a genuine 2144-byte WOTS+ signature with a single 0x00 appended returned success=true, as did the same signature with 4096 attacker-chosen 0xab bytes appended. The reference implementation in packages/runar-testing/src/crypto/wots.ts has always rejected a wrong-length signature (`if (sig.length !== LEN * N) return false`), so this was a live divergence between the two oracles, not a shared design decision. WHAT THE ATTACKER GAINED, measured rather than asserted: malleability and nothing more. The verdict is a pure function of the first 2144 bytes, so padding never rescued a tampered signature (tested: still false), never made a signature verify against a different message (still false), and prefixed junk still failed; short signatures already aborted inside OP_SPLIT. What it did buy is unbounded third-party rewriting of the unlocking script: any relaying node could append arbitrary bytes to the WOTS signature of an in-flight transaction, changing its txid without invalidating it — which breaks chains of unconfirmed spends and the pre-signed stateful continuations the stateful-wots-gate fixture exists to exercise — and inflate the transaction's size, and so lower its effective fee rate, without limit. THE FIX is a 5-byte prologue gate, OP_SIZE <2144> OP_EQUALVERIFY, emitted once per verifyWOTS at the point where the signature is already on top of the stack (net stack effect zero). 2144 = LEN(67) * N(32) is written in every tier as `67 * 32` from named WOTS+ parameters, not as a magic number; WOTS+ here has a single parameter set (w=16, n=32, len1=64, len2=3), so the bound is a constant and there is no parameter to track — unlike SLH-DSA, whose sibling BUG-011 guard derives its length per FIPS-205 parameter set. The gate follows that SLH-DSA prologue convention exactly (OP_SIZE / push / OP_EQUALVERIFY, hard failure rather than a false result), which is consistent with the primitive already aborting on a short signature. EVIDENCE FOR THE NEW BYTES, none of it self-graded: (1) the reproduction test is executed on the real Spend interpreter, and it carries two CONTROLS with teeth — a genuine correctly-sized signature must still verify, and a second real signature over a different message must still verify; setting the bound to 2145 instead of 2144 reddens BOTH controls (exit 1, 4 failures) while the attack cases flip, so an over-strict gate cannot hide here; (2) FALSIFIED per tier: deleting the three gate ops from exactly one of the seven emitters, rebuilding that tier's binary, and re-running conformance reddens exactly that tier and no other — 'majority [six tiers] vs [neutered tier] first differs at byte 13', seven times out of seven, each with a non-zero exit; (3) all seven independently written compilers regenerate these exact bytes byte-for-byte, with no cross-tier script or IR mismatch reported by the conformance runner; (4) an exhaustive sweep of all 78 conformance fixtures shows exactly 3 move and 75 are byte-unchanged, and every fixture grows by exactly +5 bytes — the gate's own width, once — which confirms the change is confined to the WOTS+ family and emits one gate per call; expected-ir.json is unchanged everywhere because the gate lives in stack lowering, below ANF.

SECTION 2 SCOPE: this fixture composes the SECTION 1 stateful covenant blob with a verifyWOTS call. R-135 adds 5 bytes inside the verifyWOTS body only; the binding blob SECTION 1 describes is byte-unchanged, and its evidence still stands for the parts of this script it covers.

Codegen change for #137 (the on-chain SLH-DSA verifier was FIPS-205 NON-CONFORMANT). Two verify-path deviations were fixed in the shared SLH-DSA emitter across all 7 tiers, and NEITHER ALONE was sufficient to accept the standard vector: (1) FIPS 205 Sec 11.2.1 -- H_msg's MGF1 seed must be R || PK.seed || SHA-256(R || PK.seed || PK.root || M); the emitter omitted the R || PK.seed prefix, which NIST added to mitigate multi-target long-message second-preimage attacks. (2) FIPS 205 Alg. 8 lines 8-11 -- wots_pkFromSig must restore the key pair address after setTypeAndClear(WOTS_PK) zeroes ADRS bytes 20-31; the emitter pushed four zero bytes and never restored the real leaf index. Evidence is an OFFICIAL KAT, not a self-golden: NIST ACVP SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s (internal) sigVer vector, tgId 31 / tcId 422, testPassed=true, vendored verbatim at conformance/runtime-vectors/slh-dsa-acvp-kat.json. The previous goldens were graded only against signatures this repo produced with the same buggy signer -- the BUG-101 self-consistency trap. Scripts shrank slightly (the PICKed key-pair address is cheaper than a 4-byte push); expected-ir.json did not move, because the change is confined to stack lowering. All 7 tiers emit byte-identical hex for this fixture (conformance 72/72 in both fold modes). This fixture is SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s (n=16, SHA-256-only per FIPS 205 Table 2) -- the EXACT parameter set the ACVP vector covers -- and it is verified END-TO-END THROUGH THE COMPILED SCRIPT, not merely through the off-chain helper, by packages/runar-testing/src/__tests__/post-quantum-slh-acvp-onchain.test.ts, which replays the NIST signature on @bsv/sdk's Spend interpreter and requires accept, plus reject on a 1-bit tamper. Both fixes were RED-proved: reverting either one individually turns that on-chain accept test red. Native Go verify is separately gated by TestOfficialKAT_SLHDSA_ACVP (packages/runar-go/crypto_kat_test.go), now an enforcing assertion rather than the xfail it replaced.

NEW-014: `&&` / `||` now SHORT-CIRCUIT on-chain. They lowered to OP_BOOLAND / OP_BOOLOR, which are binary stack ops -- both operands must already be ON the stack, so both were evaluated unconditionally. spec/semantics.md 3.7 licensed that with "This is safe in Runar because all expressions are pure (no side effects beyond assert)", but purity is not TOTALITY: 10 of the same document lists division by zero as a runtime failure, and OP_SPLIT / OP_NUM2BIN abort out of range. Evaluating the operand the source skipped therefore ABORTED the script, so the ordinary defensive guard `assert(d === 0n || (100n / d) > 1n)` compiled to a locking script the chain rejects for exactly the input the guard exists to protect -- a permanently unspendable UTXO -- while the AST interpreter (which short-circuits) reported success. `&&` / `||` now desugar to the ternary, which stack lowering already emits as real OP_IF / OP_ELSE control flow (3.9 already specified the untaken arm as unevaluated), so the moved bytes are OP_BOOLAND/OP_BOOLOR (0x9a/0x9b) becoming OP_IF/OP_ELSE/OP_ENDIF (0x63/0x67/0x68). EVIDENCE IS THE DIFFERENTIAL ORACLE, NOT A SELF-GOLDEN: the OLD bytes are REJECTED by @bsv/sdk's real Spend.validate() on inputs the source accepts. The three specific consensus rejections pinned in packages/runar-testing/src/__tests__/shortcircuit-consensus-vm.test.ts are "OP_DIV cannot divide by zero!" (d=0 through a `||` zero-guard), "OP_SPLIT requires the first stack item to be a non-negative number less than or equal to the size of the second-from-top stack item" (a guarded out-of-range substr), and "OP_NUM2BIN requires that the size expressed in the top stack item is large enough to hold the value expressed in the second-from-top stack item" (a guarded undersized num2bin). That suite pins BOTH directions for every short-circuiting case -- the input that must not reach the right operand, the input that must reach it and hold, and the input that must reach it and reject -- so a compiler that simply dropped the right operand could not pass it. All 7 tiers emit byte-identical hex and IR for this fixture in both fold modes (conformance 72/72), and the regeneration moved ONLY the six files of the three fixtures whose sources use `&&` / `||`; a control regeneration on the unpatched tree was a byte-for-byte no-op, so every moved byte is attributable to this change alone. THIS FILE: the ANF IR (the desugar happens in ANF lowering, so the IR moves too) for fixture `bitwise-ops`, whose source examples/ts/bitwise-ops/BitwiseOps.runar.ts uses six `||` guards. Its bytes move because those operators change lowering; no other behaviour of the fixture changed.

----- SECTION (2026-09-15, R-157 ecMul on-curve-or-infinity gate) -----

R-157: the ladder's correctness argument holds only for points ON the curve, every tier wrote that down, and nothing enforced it.

`ecMul(P, k)` does not compute k*P. It computes ((k mod n) + 3n)*P: the MSB-first ladder adds 3n so that a fixed high bit is always set, and +3n is a NO-OP ONLY WHEN ord(P) DIVIDES n. Cofactor 1 gives ord(P) = n for every point on the curve, so the trick is sound there and nowhere else. A point off the curve lies on some other curve y^2 = x^3 + b' whose order is unrelated to n, and the whole computation silently answers a different question.

The degenerate sub-case is worse. R-135: verifyWOTS shipped with NO signature-length gate. The emitted verifier consumes the signature 32 bytes at a time with OP_SPLIT, 67 times, then dropped whatever was left over — the TS emitter's own comment said "drop empty sigRest" without ever checking that it was empty. The reference implementation in packages/runar-testing/src/crypto/wots.ts has always rejected a wrong-length signature (`if (sig.length !== LEN * N) return false`), so this was a live divergence between the two oracles, not a shared design decision. WHAT THE ATTACKER GAINED, measured rather than asserted: malleability and nothing more. The verdict is a pure function of the first 2144 bytes, so padding never rescued a tampered signature (tested: still false), never made a signature verify against a different message (still false), and prefixed junk still failed; short signatures already aborted inside OP_SPLIT. R-120: the Merkle index was an unbounded witness and the proof remainder was dropped unread. `emitMerkleRoot` unrolls `depth` levels, consults bit i of the index at level i, never looks above bit depth-1, and then drops the index; separately it OP_SPLITs 32 bytes off the proof blob per level and dropped whatever was left. Both holes were REPRODUCED by execution before the fix, not inferred from the bytes. On the go-sdk interpreter at depth 2, indices 1, 5, 9, 1025 and -1 all returned the same root 5306f72f...6ee0f336, and proof blobs of 64, 65, 96 and 128 bytes all returned that same root. So merkleRootSha256(leaf, proof, i) authenticated nothing about i beyond its low `depth` bits -- one accepted proof was a proof for every index in the same residue class mod 2^depth -- and the proof blob had infinitely many accepted spellings.

THE NEW BYTES are two OP_VERIFY gates in stack lowering (ANF is unmoved: expected-ir.json does not change for any fixture in this commit): a prologue `OP_DUP <0> <2^depth> OP_WITHIN OP_VERIFY` bounding the index, and an epilogue `OP_SIZE <0> OP_NUMEQUALVERIFY` proving the proof blob was fully consumed. Aborting rather than reducing, because these are VALUE builtins and CL-BUG-095 set the policy that predicates clamp and flag while value producers OP_VERIFY -- reducing the index mod 2^depth would preserve today's aliasing under a politer name. A SHORT proof already aborted inside OP_SPLIT, so only the over-long direction needed closing.

R-120: the Merkle index was an unbounded witness and the proof remainder was dropped unread. `emitMerkleRoot` unrolls `depth` levels, consults bit i of the index at level i, never looks above bit depth-1, and then drops the index; separately it OP_SPLITs 32 bytes off the proof blob per level and dropped whatever was left. Both holes were REPRODUCED by execution before the fix, not inferred from the bytes. On the go-sdk interpreter at depth 2, indices 1, 5, 9, 1025 and -1 all returned the same root 5306f72f...6ee0f336, and proof blobs of 64, 65, 96 and 128 bytes all returned that same root. So merkleRootSha256(leaf, proof, i) authenticated nothing about i beyond its low `depth` bits -- one accepted proof was a proof for every index in the same residue class mod 2^depth -- and the proof blob had infinitely many accepted spellings. THE NEW BYTES are two OP_VERIFY gates in stack lowering (ANF is unmoved: expected-ir.json does not change for any fixture in this commit): a prologue `OP_DUP <0> <2^depth> OP_WITHIN OP_VERIFY` bounding the index, and an epilogue `OP_SIZE <0> OP_NUMEQUALVERIFY` proving the proof blob was fully consumed. Aborting rather than reducing, because these are VALUE builtins and CL-BUG-095 set the policy that predicates clamp and flag while value producers OP_VERIFY -- reducing the index mod 2^depth would preserve today's aliasing under a politer name. A SHORT proof already aborted inside OP_SPLIT, so only the over-long direction needed closing.
